input.short_description: Replay historical events through a pipeline to populate new destinations or catch up on missed data.
input.body:
Overview

Backfilling is the process of replaying historical events through a pipeline to populate new destinations or recover from gaps in data flow. This is useful when you add a new destination connector to an existing pipeline or need to catch up on missed events.

When to backfill

Common scenarios for backfilling include:

  • Adding a new destination to an established pipeline
  • Recovering from a service outage or data loss
  • Migrating data to a new system
  • Enriching historical data with new transformations

Backfill patterns

There are several approaches depending on your data store and pipeline configuration:

Full historical replay

Extract all historical events from your source system and replay them through the pipeline. This ensures complete data consistency but may take significant time depending on your data volume.

Time-windowed backfill

Divide the historical period into smaller time windows and replay each batch separately. This approach helps manage resource usage and allows you to verify correctness at each stage.

Cursored backfill

Use cursor-based pagination to incrementally backfill events. This is efficient for systems that support cursor-based access and allows you to track progress and resume if interrupted.

Best practices

  • Test backfill logic in a non-production environment first
  • Monitor pipeline performance during backfills to avoid overwhelming destination systems
  • Use time windows to manage resource consumption
  • Track backfill progress and verify event counts match expectations
  • Consider deduplication if events might be processed multiple times

input.short_description: Route events from a single source to multiple destination connectors in parallel.
input.body:
Overview

Fan-out is a pattern where events from a single source connector are routed to multiple destination connectors simultaneously. This allows you to keep multiple systems in sync, create redundancy, or distribute data to specialized consumers.

When to fan-out

Fan-out is useful when you need to:

  • Synchronize data across multiple systems (data warehouses, analytics platforms, CRMs)
  • Create redundant copies for high-availability requirements
  • Distribute data to different teams or departments
  • Feed multiple machine learning models with the same feature data

Fan-out patterns

Broadcast pattern

Send identical events to all destinations. This is the simplest approach and works well when all consumers need the same data shape.

Content-based routing

Use transformations to route events to different destinations based on event content. For example, send customer events to a CRM and transaction events to a data warehouse.

Filtered fan-out

Each destination receives a filtered subset of events. Use transformation steps to filter before routing, or configure destination-specific filtering rules.

Configuration

To configure fan-out in Godzilla, simply connect the same source connector to multiple destination connectors in your pipeline topology. Godzilla will automatically fan out events to all connected destinations.

Best practices

  • Monitor each destination's health independently
  • Use error handling and dead-letter queues to manage destination failures
  • Consider rate limits on downstream systems when fanning out to many destinations
  • Use transformations to normalize data to each destination's expected format
  • Plan for ordering guarantees if consumers require event ordering
